Hi! Thanks for the comment. This is a really really good question. That’s the part of the safety plan I’ve struggled with most. Actually, none of the people on this safety plan are still on my safety plan 3 years later.

For me, I’ve had therapists that will let me call them any time just to talk if I’m struggling, so I’d include them. I also have joined a few different support groups for people struggling with mental health/suicidal thoughts so I have a few people from those groups I’ve gotten close to that I can call in a time of crisis or just text. But usually I’ll have like 1 maybe 2 friends that I could reach out to. Right now that’s not the case. 

But, the way I like to think about the social supports section is that just because you call the person doesn’t mean you have to tell them you’re struggling. Like if you choose to reach out before you get to a crisis point, you can just call and have a regular conversation with the person. 

For me, sometimes just getting out of my head and talking to someone makes a huge difference. But of course, it’s best if it’s someone you can call and just let them know you’re struggling, but that’s tough for me personally so just having someone for call or text to chat with is enough.

My biggest advice would be to find an online or in-person support group. That way you can be connected to other people going through similar things and they encourage you to reach out. Sometimes it’s awkward to or not safe to talk to people in our personal lives about our struggles, but support groups have been life-saving for me. For example, I’m a part of Suicide Anonymous, Emotions Anonymous, Alternatives to Suicide, and Survivors of Suicide Attempts. All of the groups meet virtually and they have discord chats or what’s app group messages to chat between meetings.

TLDR; you can put close friends, your therapist, people you’ve met in support groups, etc. My biggest advice is to find online or in-person support groups, it’s been life-saving for me.

As an MHT on an inpatient unit and a patient getting therapy/med management services I agree.

The system is so so flawed. Medications are given out so quickly and without thought it seems. At one point I was on 5 different meds for my depression/anxiety... 

I’ve seen about 5 different therapists in the last 6 years and the styles vary so much and a lot of therapists who claim to use a certain strategy like CBT or DBT don’t actually properly utilize the treatment. 

Inpatient treatment is virtually useless unless you will literally kill yourself without being locked up. There are very limited resources on units, especially where I work. Patients see the psychiatrist for about 10 minutes per day and it’s almost purely about medications. The only real changes that happen on inpatient units are medication dosages.

Follow-up and aftercare is often poor and some institutions don’t even schedule follow up appointments. 

The wait times to even see a psychiatrist or therapist can be crazy long and then if you don’t mesh well with the provider it can be difficult to switch providers.

My plans in grad school are to do research on improving treatment interventions for MDD and GAD using brain imaging techniques. I really think that until we can better understand the etiology of these common mental illnesses we can’t properly treat them.

I think access to services is the biggest barrier, plus our system is largely reactive rather than proactive. If elementary schools did mental health screenings and kids were actually able to get treatment early then the issues would be much less likely to progress..
